papers.title: Spatial zoning effects on short-term taxi demand prediction: A machine learning and deep learning analysis
Is X-minute city accessibility associated with mode-specific travel behavior? District-level evidence from Munich
papers.abstract: The X-minute city is built on the idea that proximity to essential daily destinations should support more sustainable travel and improve urban livability, yet this behavioral claim has rarely been tested directly with observed mobility data at the city district level. This paper addresses that gap by providing the first empirical test of whether X-minute city accessibility conditions are associated with modal split across walking, cycling, public transport and car use in Munich’s 25 administrative districts. It does so using the city’s district-level travel survey data, allowing accessibility to be linked not just to where opportunities are located, but to how residents actually travel. Accessibility is measured using Geo Open Accessibility Tool indicators, including mean travel times and 15-minute reachability coverage across six destination categories. These measures are then combined with district-level modal sharesfrom the 2023 System of Representative Transport Surveys. Using Spearman rank correlations and population-weighted regression models, the paper shows that accessibility is strongly associated with walking and car use, with destination proximity alone explaining over 85% of the variance in both modes. Cycling shows a weaker but statistically significant relationship, while public transport shares are not significantly related to proximity-based accessibility to public transport stations, suggesting that network connectivity and service frequency are more important for that mode. Overall, the findings provide district-scale empirical evidence for the behavioral patterns of the X-minute city across transport modes, while showing that explanatory power differs substantially between them.
